descriptions.NUR18791: Of the monument, currently destroyed, only some worked ashlar stones remain, indicating that the tomb type was coursed in isodomic masonry.
descriptions.NUR17909: Tomb of which the orthostats of the corridor emerge from the ground. No stele or exedra are visible.
descriptions.NUR8294: The tomb was restored in 1993, reusing the exedra and the other orthostats and putting them back in their original positions; they were sometimes deteriorated or broken but still in situ. The monument, which shows two different construction phases, was built in both phases in the Early Bronze Age and was used for funerary purposes only during the first phase.
descriptions.NUR11626: Interesting giants' tomb with a bilitic arched stele, of which only the lower part with a door remains. The exedra and the burial chamber are also present.
descriptions.NUR11877: Dug in 1996–97. Nearby, numerous menhir statues were found, some of which are partially preserved at the Samugheo textile art museum.
descriptions.NUR12206: It is a giants' tomb with a collapsed structure and in relative abandonment.
descriptions.NUR12533: At the foot of the hill, once used as a stone quarry, inside the built-up area of Monastir, in the south-western part, near Via Progresso no. 80, a giants' tomb was found during an archaeological excavation, which yielded numerous human bone remains.
descriptions.NUR11613: The tomb, of dolmenic type and aligned on a west-east axis, preserves only the burial chamber, part of the exedra with the large arched stele, while the outer profile of the tomb and therefore its thickness cannot be detected. Noted by Lamarmora, who in the Atlas documents the stele already broken, as it appears today.
descriptions.NUR17167: Remains of a giants' tomb, of which the base courses remain.
descriptions.NUR11646: Nuragic dolmen burial, with the funerary corridor remaining, composed of finely finished basalt slabs, without steles.
descriptions.NUR17265: It is in poor conservation condition. Position verified with GPS.
descriptions.NUR11722: The burial stands on the flat summit of Planu Borgolo, about 50 m east of the line of the SS131, which separates it from the settlement to which it belongs. The tomb's layout and the funerary corridor, formed by several large orthostatic slabs, especially at the far end, are still discernible; only a few elements of the exedra survive.
descriptions.NUR11925: Giants' tomb, dolmenic, completely exposed, with only a trapezoidal stele and part of the original exedra remaining
descriptions.NUR12203: A burial of the Nuragic period with isodomic masonry. Of the tomb, partially demolished, only the burial corridor, the apse, and some elements of the left arm of the exedra remain.
descriptions.NUR10647: Remains of the megalithic construction were revealed during a survey at the nearby Perdu Lodde nuraghe by a local shepherd.
descriptions.NUR19474: Giants' tomb Sa Canna, in the Sàrrala area of Tertenia but administratively belonging to one of the many enclaves in the zone (39.61237 N 9.63864 E). This was my first encounter with a tomb built of schist, a stone used only sporadically for this type of monument. It is of the coursed type, considered more recent than the 'dolmenic' or 'arched stele' type, and has an elegant exedra — although it lacks the dentilled ashlar characteristic of the more refined examples — standing 2.55 m high at its apex. The tomb shows some gaps due to clandestine disturbance (the missing ashlar from the left arm of the exedra is clearly visible), which prevent the exact width of the semicircle from being determined, though it can be assessed as having a slight curvature. The chamber, not very large, is 6.75 metres long measured at the outer threshold and 6.40 metres at the inner threshold, and is distinguished by a perfect ogive with a descending height from 1.95 m at the entrance to 1.40 m (presumed, since the clandestine excavation has disturbed the basal paving) at the rear, where traces of ancient plastering seem to be detectable (unless this is due to a neoformation of clay caused by the loss of the corridor's waterproofing — which, on the other hand, remains intact for almost its entire length). The entrance doorway is trapezoidal (50 cm wide at the base and 60 cm at the top), 57 cm high, and easily passable. This is therefore one of the tombs in which it is clear that access from the top of the corridor was not possible, as most island archaeologists maintain (on the other side of the 'barricade' stood the great Ercole Contu, who in my opinion took a more scientific approach to the question), since there is no possibility of removing any ashlars from the corridor to allow such hypothetical access. The tomb almost certainly belongs to a settlement located about 500 metres away as the crow flies, on another saddle of the same ridge, of which only a few remains can be identified today: a non-canonical type of nuraghe and a few surrounding traces attributable to huts (the area is also known as Serra 'e Mari, and a boundary stone — the municipalities concerned are Lanusei and Arzana — was placed on the nuraghe in 1953).
descriptions.NUR10346: Collective burial of the Nuragic period. In very poor condition of conservation.
descriptions.NUR11460: Right next to the electric company village there are two nuraghi and this exceptional giants' tomb belonging to them, called Pira Onne. Here too the stele with its three recesses for the trinity that usually stood above the exedra of coursed masonry stands out; the blocks are slightly squared.
descriptions.NUR9751: The giants' tomb Sa Fache e s'Altare is a corridor tomb with an arched stele.
descriptions.NUR12175:
The tomb was part of a funerary complex originally composed of four megalithic burials set a short distance from one another and very close to the Ilòi and Logula nuraghi.

The present road alignment has split the small necropolis of giants' tombs built to serve the villages along a network of transhumance routes. It is a dolmenic tomb, originally furnished with a bilithic arched stele with a doorway at its base, placed at the centre of the exedra.
descriptions.NUR12176:
The tomb was part of a funerary complex originally composed of four megalithic burials set a short distance from one another and very close to the Ilòi and Logula nuraghi.

The present road alignment has split the small necropolis of giants' tombs built to serve the villages along a network of transhumance routes. It is a dolmenic tomb, originally furnished with a bilithic arched stele with a doorway at its base, placed at the centre of the exedra.
descriptions.NUR16871: Giants' tomb in miniature, very small
descriptions.NUR11442:
Situated a short distance from the rural church of S. Gavino and about a hundred metres to the north-west of the Nuraghe Toscono, with which it had a close cultural relationship, the tomb of Santu Bainzu is of the dolmenic type with a monolithic arched stele, aligned along the SE-NW axis and with the entrance to the south-east.

It was recorded by Lamarmora, whose drawing still shows the orthostats of the exedra in situ, whereas they are no longer present in a later plan sketch by Mackenzie.
descriptions.NUR18118: Giants' tomb in a state of complete abandonment, located just a few dozen metres from the nuraghe.
descriptions.NUR10588: Of the two giants' tombs, both relatively eroded, the burial chamber and the exedra are identifiable.
descriptions.NUR10587: Of the two giants' tombs, both relatively eroded, the burial chamber and the exedra are identifiable.
descriptions.NUR11715: Of this burial only the stele and part of the exedra remain.
descriptions.NUR12411: The giants' tomb of Sas Melas stands about 200 metres as the crow flies from the nuraghe of the same name. The tomb is completely buried and in very poor condition; only a few orthostatic stones are visible, protruding just a few centimetres.
descriptions.NUR11029: The giants' tomb of “Sa Sedda 'e Sena”, known as 'Sa Tanchitta', has the peculiarity of having been built in the Nuragic period by adapting a much older funerary structure, dating to the Early Bronze Age (1800–1600 BC) of the allée couverte type. Of this funerary monument, the burial chamber, about 10 metres long, can still be observed today.
descriptions.NUR11372: Two giants' tombs adjacent, from two different construction periods. The first is of dolmenic type, the second is coursed (with opposed courses).
descriptions.NUR11373: Two giants' tombs adjacent, from two different construction periods. The first is of dolmenic type, the second is coursed (with opposed courses).
descriptions.NUR11881: Beyond the two monumental giants' tombs, unique and clearly visible and of exceptional workmanship, three other tombs have been identified. For anyone familiar with Nuragic buildings and settlement patterns this means the existence of a community of several hundred people that had needed to multiply its necropolises.
descriptions.NUR11880: Beyond the two monumental giants' tombs, unique and clearly visible and of exceptional workmanship, three other tombs have been identified. For anyone familiar with Nuragic buildings and settlement patterns this means the existence of a community of several hundred people that had needed to multiply its necropolises.
descriptions.NUR21003: Feature covered by vegetation of indistinct nature
descriptions.NUR11742:
Dimensions: h. 1.50 m; length 10.50 m; width 1.40 m.

The tomb stands on a small rise whose gentle slopes are currently used for vine cultivation. The left wing of the exedra survives, formed by large blocks that decrease in size from the entrance towards the lateral ends. The entrance, lacking the stele, shows an interesting arrangement for its setting: a shaped granite block on which a stele presumably rested.
descriptions.NUR12396:
Hidden among the vegetation, very little of the tomb remains.

It is of the coursed type and the walls of the burial chamber were built with isodomic masonry; the monument, oriented to the south-east, has a total length, measured as far as the chord of the exedra, of 7.60 m, and a maximum width of 3.15 m. One arm of the tomb and the exedra are partially visible.
descriptions.NUR11736: The tomb, situated about 300 metres north of the nuraghe of the same name, is in a good state of preservation. The entrance, facing east, gives access to a rectangular tomb about 10 metres long and about 1.20 metres high, built of well-shaped ashlars laid in regular courses.
descriptions.NUR8637: The monument takes its name from the ancient name of the area where it stands (Nixias) and from the unusual hole on the right of the great stele, which was thought (perhaps wrongly) to have been used in historic times for tethering horses. The monument is of considerable interest because it is a rare example of a giants' tomb with an arched stele in the centre-south of the island.
descriptions.NUR11627: The monument was built in two phases. In the first, dating to the Bonnanaro culture period, the allée couverte tomb – a kind of elongated dolmen – was constructed; later, around 1600 BC, it was turned into a giants' tomb with exedra and stele, traces of which you can still see.
descriptions.NUR15762: A burial of the Nuragic period, only faintly legible in its plan. Only a fragment of the arched stele remains.
descriptions.NUR11643: What remains of a dolmenic giants' tomb completely collapsed, mainly consisting of the vertical elements and the surrounding foundations.
descriptions.NUR12413: "Giants' tomb of Torrà, near the tributary Rio Torrà of Rio di Posada; few remains of a large cist or corridor can be seen, almost completely dismantled. On land belonging to Antonio Nanu, it was Giovanni." With this brief description and some geographical inaccuracies (the Riu Thorra is not a tributary of the Posada but of the Mannu, which is in turn a tributary of the Posada river), Taramelli reported the presence of the giants' tomb of Thorra, without however mentioning the nearby nuraghe.
descriptions.NUR18192: Apart from a large worked slab, nothing of the probable tomb remains, except a heap of stones.
descriptions.NUR12204: The Nuragic-period burial is currently crossed lengthwise by a dry-stone wall and its ground plan is not fully legible. The left-hand perimeter and the lower part of the bilithic stele can nevertheless be made out.
descriptions.NUR10709: The tomb extends along a north-east/south-west major axis 5.50 m long and has its entrance opening to the south-west at the centre of a semicircular exedra that has almost entirely disappeared. The rear apse was probably straight-sided, but the closing masonry has not survived. It should be noted that the tomb is still largely buried, giving the impression that what is currently visible is actually the uppermost courses, lacking their covering.
descriptions.NUR11466: A burial of the Nuragic period. Of the monument, partially hidden by vegetation and collapse debris, only the outer perimeter, the funerary corridor, and part of the exedra remain visible.
descriptions.NUR6800: These are three baetyls of truncated-conical shape, about a metre and a half high with a diameter of about 60–80 cm, lying on the right-hand side of the tomb. At some unknown date the central baetyl was overturned and turned into a trough.
descriptions.NUR15657: A burial of the Nuragic period, almost completely destroyed. The ground plan of the tomb and a few worked ashlars are visible on the ground. In particular, two monolithic arches belonging to the apsidal part of the tomb lie a short distance away.
descriptions.NUR15660: Only traces of the structure remain, as it has been completely dismantled.
descriptions.NUR18703: Only a short stretch of the first basal course survives on the side by the farmhouse; around the monument there are two small to medium-sized granite slabs that appear to be pieces of the stele.
descriptions.NUR12191: The tomb, of dolmenic structure, is now visible only in the burial corridor, the entrance and the right wing of the exedra. Of the tomb body, a single row of medium-sized stones forming the left side of the burial just emerges from the ground.
descriptions.NUR18812: Of the monument, currently destroyed, only a single ashlar with a curved profile belonging to the apsidal area remains, indicating that the tomb type was coursed in isodomic masonry.
descriptions.NUR16987: Collective burial of the Nuragic period. The structure has been largely destroyed. Some alignments of stones relating to the corridor and the exedra help to identify the layout of the monument.
descriptions.NUR16985: Collective burial of the Nuragic period. The monument is completely covered by a layer of mastic but the terminal section of the corridor is still visible.
descriptions.NUR16982: A collective burial of the Nuragic period. The structure is hard to see because, besides being swallowed by the usual thicket of mastic, it is also covered with small stones from the clearance of the surrounding ground.
descriptions.NUR16981: A collective burial of the Nuragic period. The structure has been largely destroyed, as well as covered by vegetation and rubble.
descriptions.NUR18652: The monument is practically destroyed and very little of the ground plan can be made out on the ground. Nevertheless, a fragment of the arched stele incorporated in the adjacent dry-stone wall confirms the existence of the tomb.
descriptions.NUR12338: Giants' tomb, dolmenic, partially collapsed, with only the perimetral orthostats and a lapidary lintel remaining.
descriptions.NUR12337: Giants' tomb, dolmenic, partially collapsed, with only the perimetral orthostats and a lapidary lintel remaining.
descriptions.NUR8580:
It consists of an apsidal corridor set on an exedra with a narrow bench. In the centre is a small lintelled doorway with jambs and a threshold. The roof is a pointed vault.

Excavations have uncovered the remains of numerous human skeletons, deposited one on top of another, evidence of its use as a collective burial, whose size is also the origin of the name. Tradition holds that these burials must have belonged to gigantic beings.
descriptions.NUR18921:
A burial of the Nuragic period in very poor condition of conservation.

The corridor and, with difficulty, the exedra are visible in the isodomic masonry type.
descriptions.NUR11889:
A burial of the Nuragic period. The external profile, the funerary corridor and the exedra can be observed.

The construction technique is regular coursed masonry using sub-squared polygonal blocks.

The tomb has the peculiarity of being unusually oriented towards the south-west, and is also very close to its reference nuraghe (about 25 m).

The monument lies in the municipal territory of Villagrande Strisaili (OG).
descriptions.NUR11025:
It is also known as Sa Pinnettedda.

The circumstances of its discovery and the materials recovered place the monument chronologically at the end of phase II of the Nuragic civilization (1500–1200 BC),
descriptions.NUR10875: The tomb is svettato and consists of an orthostatic structure in courses. Part of the exedra, the architrave portal, the funerary corridor, and part of the apse are visible. Length about 12 m.
descriptions.NUR10862: A burial chamber of about 11 m in length remains. The tomb is missing its top. The exedra and the abside are still visible.
descriptions.NUR11021: The Giants' Tombs of Mont'Ollastu (Villamassargia) have been the subject of past archaeological excavations and have yielded ceramic artifacts visible at the Archaeological Museum of Cagliari.
descriptions.NUR15349: Man-made structure submerged by an artificial lake
descriptions.NUR15347: Man-made structure submerged by the artificial lake
descriptions.NUR15351: Man-made structure submerged by the artificial lake
descriptions.NUR15353: Man-made structure submerged by the artificial lake
descriptions.NUR15355: Man-made structure submerged by the artificial lake
descriptions.NUR15357: Man-made structure submerged by the artificial lake
descriptions.NUR1943: The remains of the funerary structure are completely covered by a thicket of mastic. A circular hut built in recent times on the tomb remains is present; part of the exedra, formed by five basalt boulders arranged in a semicircle, is visible.
descriptions.NUR14771:
The tomb is in a poor state of preservation, hidden by vegetation, and only "recently" has a fire partly revealed the structure.

The most visible part is the exedra, in particular the lower section of the bilithic stele, while the corridor is marked by a few stones emerging from the ground and a covering slab.
descriptions.NUR10861: The tomb has its top missing; it has a rectangular plan and no longer shows any trace of the apse. Its length is about 12 m. At present some blocks of the left arm of the exedra, the entrance, and the perimeter wall can be observed.
descriptions.NUR10860: Svettated tomb with walls emerging only a few centimetres. Width of about 4.50 m, calculable length of about 7 m. A burial chamber, an apse, and an external perimeter wall are discernible.
descriptions.NUR18646: A burial of the Nuragic period of dolmenic type, built with stone orthostats set vertically and covered with horizontal slabs. The corridor of the tomb is visible, while the elements of the exedra should be incorporated in the dry-stone wall built on the façade. Also on the façade lies the beautiful arched stele, overturned and, unfortunately, fragmented.
descriptions.NUR17208:
Only shaped ashlars of the monument can be identified, from which it can be established that the tomb was of the coursed type in isodomic masonry.

Some of the ashlars (perhaps those belonging to the exedra) are incorporated into the walling of a recent hut, and others lie scattered nearby, hidden by vegetation. In particular, the so-called dentilled stele of considerable size is present.

The baetyls now placed in the forecourt of the Church of Santa Caterina appear to come from it.
descriptions.NUR17210: It is in poor conservation state, severely damaged by excavation and earth movement. It retains in the apsidal area a baetyl with a single "ocular" opening, not fully defined.
descriptions.NUR17225: Of the coursed monument in isodomic masonry, the tomb body, the corridor defined by several shaped and well-fitted ashlars, the apse, and part of the exedra survive. A shaped ashlar, but probably damaged, may constitute the so-called dentilled stele.
descriptions.NUR11639: Part of the monument retains the funerary corridor; six courses of stones remain on the right side and only two on the left, with a maximum length of 7.70 m and a width of 1 m.
descriptions.NUR15743: There are three giants' tombs, of which the first is the most important and in the best state of preservation.
descriptions.NUR14241: The tomb is built in isodomic masonry with a coursed façade. The burial chamber, squat and symmetrical, apsidal, tapers slightly into a broad semicircular exedra edged with benches, facing SSE. Of the monument, in local basalt, the basal course of the burial chamber survives, part of the basal slabs of the façade and of the bench seat, and a good part of the extradosed roofing of monolithic arches.
descriptions.NUR11645:
Funerary structure of the Nuragic period.

Entry form to be completed.

The monument is located in the territory of the comune of Norbello (OR).
descriptions.NUR11638: Of the monument only the corridor tomb remains, which has five courses of stones to the west and six to the east, with a maximum length of 7.40 m and a width of 1 m.
descriptions.NUR18914: Two giants' tombs, probably associated with the nearby Prizzada nuraghe.
descriptions.NUR16979: A collective burial of the Nuragic period. The monument, like the other tombs in the area, is in very poor condition. The corridor formed by two parallel courses of stones is still legible, and the outer profile can be recognised in some stretches. Some regular ashlars incorporated in the surrounding dry-stone walls may belong to the tomb.
descriptions.NUR15736: Of the practically destroyed monument, the outer outline of the tomb body and the exedra are still visible on the ground. Shaped ashlars worked on their exposed faces lie on the ground, showing that the tomb was of the coursed type in isodomic masonry. During the last site visit (Jan. 2012) it was found that the two so-called dentilled stelae that lay next to the burial are no longer present.
descriptions.NUR11968:
A burial of the Nuragic period. A monument of considerable size in a good state of preservation, legible in all its components except the entrance area, which has now been altered and retains only two residual fragments of the original stele.

The construction technique is of the coursed type, using polygonal blocks of granite.
descriptions.NUR11971:
The monument is in a fair state of preservation despite the roots of the holm oak that overshadows it undermining its stability.

The burial corridor, built of polygonal blocks in courses, still retains almost all of its roofing, while the tomb body is defined by the mound that covers it. The exedra of dolmenic type is more clearly legible, although it lacks the stele; it consists of orthostats set vertically into the ground.

enclosed by a dry-stone wall.
descriptions.NUR11969:
A burial of the Nuragic period. The tomb body can be identified, partly hidden by the covering soil, together with the funerary corridor and the exedra.

The construction technique is coursed, using sub-squared polygonal blocks of granite.
descriptions.NUR11970: A burial of the Nuragic period. The monument, of small size, is identifiable only by the funerary corridor, while the other parts (still buried or destroyed) that composed it are not visible.
descriptions.NUR10919: Giants' tomb Sa Grutta 'e Su Bandiu
descriptions.NUR11653:
A burial of the Nuragic period. The tomb is completely engulfed in a thicket of mastic, but through the vegetation the terminal part of the burial corridor can be made out.

The monument lies in the municipal territory of Sedilo (OR).
descriptions.NUR15732:
Of the practically destroyed monument only the burial corridor remains, consisting of a depression in the ground, and numerous shaped ashlars indicating that the tomb was of the coursed type in isodomic masonry.

Among the ashlars, which are very carefully worked, one can observe the so-called dentilled stele of considerable size, and a monolithic arch belonging to the apsidal area.
descriptions.NUR17726: The giants' tomb is located in the south-west direction relative to the homonymous nuraghe, of which only the tomb corridor remains.
descriptions.NUR15754:
The monument stands about twenty metres from a second giants' tomb and about 200 metres from the eponymous nuraghe; it is not traceable in the outer perimeter because of its very poor state of preservation.

A fragment of an arched stele (height 0.46 m; width 1.25 m) with a raised frame, 12 cm wide on the left and 15–17 cm on the right, reused in the paving of the nearby church of Santa Sabina, probably belongs to this tomb.
descriptions.NUR15751:
The monument lies about 200 metres from the nuraghe of the same name.

The tomb has been partly demolished with the removal of all the worked ashlars that faced the burial chamber.

Nevertheless, despite the very poor state of preservation, the usual ground plan of this tomb type can still be read on the ground: a rectangular body with an apsidal rear, a semicircular exedra at the front, and a rectangular burial chamber.
descriptions.NUR10916: A collective burial of the Nuragic period. The monument lies next to a farm track that may have caused its damage; it is covered by vegetation, but its corridor and wall structure of courses of roughly squared granite stones can still be seen.
descriptions.NUR11649: Giants' tomb immersed in vegetation and eroded
descriptions.NUR12300: The giants' tomb of Sa Presone 1 has a semicircular exedra with a coursed façade. On the right side of the apsidal burial chamber, which is roofed with slabs, a small niche raised above the floor can be seen; it was used for placing offerings or a body in a crouched position.
descriptions.NUR12299: Sa Presone 2 today preserves only traces of the chamber. Among the scattered stones around it, a dentilled ashlar with three recesses has been identified.
descriptions.NUR12298:
It is practically destroyed. The few remains that allow it to be identified consist of two courses of stones, just emerging from the ground, that define the tomb corridor. In the area of the exedra (itself more guessed at than actually present) lies the so-called dentilled ashlar, not in its original position; its presence indicates that the burial was built with squared ashlars laid in courses, like the nearby Sa Presone II.

The monument lies in the municipality of Bultei (SS).
descriptions.NUR17720: The monument retains a good part of the internal corridor. The outer wall face can be traced as far as the exedra, of which the right-hand side is visible, while on the left there are only two upright stones corresponding to the entrance. A short distance away lies the megalithic stele, unfortunately cut, and what appears to be the closing slab.
descriptions.NUR15616: Giants' tomb, of which the base ashlar stones remain, one slab of the stele, and one from the abside.
descriptions.NUR15618: Coursed tomb, the shape of which is difficult to determine.
descriptions.NUR21184: Giants' tomb built of basalt ashlar
descriptions.NUR20332: The tomb is covered by enormous flat lithic slabs, including one longer than four metres.
descriptions.NUR18816: A collective burial of the Nuragic period. The monument has recently been brought to light after the vegetation covering it was cleared. Besides the coursed-stone corridor, the lower part of the large stele also survives.
descriptions.NUR11030:
A burial of the Nuragic period. The monument is practically destroyed. On the ground one can make out a course of the stones that formed the funerary corridor and blocks belonging to the exedra.

The most visible distinctive element is the terminal slab of the funerary corridor, still in its original position. The construction technique must have been of the coursed type, using polygonal blocks.
descriptions.NUR18568:
The megalithic monument, 13.5 m long according to the 2005 survey, does not depart from the traditional model. The long corridor was entered through a doorway cut into a generally arched stele, flanked on either side by stelae of decreasing height joined together (exedra).

Despite the collapse of the vault, the corridor is still preserved; the tomb entrance, however, is covered by a dense mastic bush, which prevents verification of the stele's integrity.
descriptions.NUR18925:
The monument is in very poor condition and only the terminal part of the corridor can be seen on the ground.

The construction technique was isodomic, with squared ashlars worked on the exposed faces.
descriptions.NUR21013: The Nuragic construction lies in a striking area above Lake Flumendosa. It is hard to reach for two reasons: you must find the path that links the Sa Scala e Trinched'assu waterfall to the Sa Ucca 'e is Canis giants' tomb and, above all, locate the tomb's exedra, which is literally submerged by extremely dense vegetation. Almost the entire corridor of the Nuragic construction survives in good condition, except for the final apsidal stretch, which is missing its covering slab.
descriptions.NUR19562: The monument has been badly damaged by a thorough and indiscriminate clearance operation. Beneath the many piled ashlars that cover the structure, the corridor and one wing of the exedra appear to be distinguishable. Among the ashlars (which show that the tomb was of the coursed, isodomic type), made with great care, the so-called dentilled stele and several curvilinear-profile elements belonging to the apsidal area can be observed.
descriptions.NUR11714: A burial of the Nuragic period of the so-called isodomic type. Of the tomb, practically destroyed, only the outer wall face and the terminal stone of the corridor are visible. A few other squared and well-finished elements on the exposed parts lie nearby.
descriptions.NUR12936: The tomb, of dolmenic type and now very ruined, preserves only part of the burial corridor and the outer profile, and some orthostats of the exedra, which is completely demolished. Among the stones lying overturned in the exedra area, a large slab stands out for its size: 2.50 m long, 1.25 m wide and 0.80 m thick; it may be part of the arched stele.
descriptions.NUR18922: A collective burial of the Nuragic period of dolmenic type. Of the tomb, now completely destroyed, the exedra and the apse are partially legible, while some fragments of the arched stele are present both on the facade and in the surroundings.
descriptions.NUR12036: Of the monument, of the coursed type made of polygonal granite blocks, the corridor and part of the external profile of the burial chamber are visible.
descriptions.NUR10762: Near the nuraghe Arrubiu are located two giants' tombs, one of which yielded a sword.
descriptions.NUR10710: It was built right at the base of the rocky outcrop on which the nuraghe Is Berritta stands. The only visible portion is perhaps the apsidal section, while the exedra has not been identified.
descriptions.NUR11459:
A burial of the Nuragic period.

There is hardly any need to describe it, so clearly is it visible in the satellite photograph.

The construction technique is of the coursed type, and the south-west alignment is worth noting, as it is not very common in giants' tombs.
descriptions.NUR18911:
At the foot of the hill on which the nuraghe Su Gattu stands, the remains of a burial in granite are visible.

Of the giants' tomb a stretch of the apse and part of the rectangular chamber bounded by large granite boulders survive, while outside the remains of the peristalith emerge.
descriptions.NUR15393: Giants' tomb belonging to the same named nuraghe. Very poor state of conservation.
descriptions.NUR7511:
A nuraghe, a menhir, a wall, and finally a domus de janas with a façade.

Ivano Sotgiu, in love with his own village, was out gathering asparagus when he reported this site where, within a couple of hundred metres, there are monuments dating from the Abealzu culture, between 2700 and 2400 BC, perhaps earlier with the menhir, the Early Bronze Age with the Nuragic wall, the Bronze Age and up to the Roman period, marked by the probable tombs.
descriptions.NUR7144: The tomb consists of a single chamber with a central pillar, while the walls contain various niches and a funerary bed with cushions at both ends. It is thought to date to the early medieval period. It is currently undergoing consolidation work that prevents visits.
descriptions.NUR6842: Three menhirs of decreasing height and size, representing a triad or "a family". The menhirs are set upon a lapidary circle.
descriptions.NUR10192: During the earthworks for the road that leads from Santu Miali down to the church of Santa Maria de Aidos, a burial was destroyed that was probably a giants' tomb or perhaps a medieval tomb. A dark trachyte lintel can still be seen in its original position.
descriptions.NUR15994:
It is in very poor condition.

Probable location.
descriptions.NUR10464: The exceptional nature of the Pranu Siara site lies in particular in the fact that the tomb is not isolated but forms part of an extensive necropolis perfectly aligned for several hundred metres and overlooked, at the change in level, by a kind of fortified enclosure that appears to protect the plateau, following settlement models of a similar type documented in the north-western area of the island, in the Olmedo and Castelsardo zones.
descriptions.NUR18884: The megalithic tomb lies further on, in a small clearing. Of the monument, which consists of a short burial corridor of pink trachyte slabs, only the basal course remains; the entrance is flanked by two carefully worked rectangular slabs, while the outer wall face, following the profile of the burial corridor, is built of vertical slabs with a fill of small stones.
descriptions.NUR11934: Giants' tomb. It is a giants' tomb with dolmenic cover.
descriptions.NUR8690: A singular funerary monument, a prehistoric tomb entirely cut into the rock. Discovered not many years ago, archaeologists regard it as a collective burial datable to the end of the Middle Bronze Age and therefore include it among the Nuragic-period giants' tombs. Its structure, however, is completely different from the usual giants' tomb types, both the coursed ones and those with a stele.
descriptions.NUR20536: Catalogued as a probable Roman-period tomb, lined. A superficial part of the monument is visible, next to a hollow in the ground, with a granite lintel and, beneath it, three walls of small and medium ashlars forming dry-stone masonry. It recalls the features of a spring.
descriptions.NUR12859: The only tomb in the territory of Dolianova attributed to the Bonnanaro culture and dated to 2200–1800 BC. Pottery, two tripods and a cup were found here. The tomb was destroyed during quarry work.
descriptions.NUR20067: "In a field at Luras there are giants' tombs, indeed there are four in the same plot, something I believe is more unique than rare. This site has been known for a long time; one tomb has been almost completely destroyed over the years. Both the Superintendency and the municipality have been informed, but no one has ever lifted a finger" (report).
descriptions.NUR8354:
Collective tombs of the Nuragic period, 1600–1800 BC, built in the final phase of the Middle Bronze Age, 1500 BC, and used until the Final Bronze Age phase, 1100–900 BC.

The elongated burial chamber has side walls of limestone blocks laid in corbelled courses, closed at the far end by a slab set on edge. The outer wall face is apsidal at the rear. The entrance, facing east in Tomb no. 1 and south-east in Tomb no. 2, is preceded by a semicircular exedra space.
descriptions.NUR2251:
A veritable necropolis of giants' tombs – it comprises four or perhaps five burials, two of which have an arched stele, and they are still preserved in good condition.

The main burial has a broad arched exedra – with barely indicated wings – that joins the tomb body without a break, with a concave-convex wall face.
descriptions.NUR13623:
Four giants' tombs, set a short distance from one another and in varying states of preservation. They are built of local limestone blocks and measure a little over 10 metres in length, except for one.

Because of illicit excavations, no intact stratigraphic context was recovered. It was nevertheless possible to identify a sequence datable from the advanced Middle Bronze Age to the Recent Bronze Age.
descriptions.NUR12537: Site where the oldest human skeletons in all of Sardinia have been found (8500–9000 BC).
descriptions.NUR12188:
It is in a poor state of preservation.

It is a proto-nuraghe; the tower survives to a maximum height of 5.50 m.

Within a radius of 400 m there are three giants' tombs, a Nuragic spring, and five baetyls.
descriptions.NUR15770: Two giants' tombs located a few tens of metres apart.
descriptions.NUR10801: The ashlars making up the tomb, largely buried, are of various types: limestone, basalt and even granite can be seen. A hole lets us see several metres of the side walls and a couple of limestone roofing slabs placed to the west. The right-hand side of the exedra is visible, though not clearly because it is buried; I have tried to document it as fully as possible. To the east, beyond a few trees, stands one of the stelae that were placed at the entrance of giants' tombs, at the centre of the exedra.
descriptions.NUR12382: Two giants' tombs located near the homonymous nuraghe and the nuragic village. A dolmen is attested nearby.
descriptions.NUR16881: Of the monument, now destroyed, only two alignments of roughly squared sandstone blocks that define the corridor are just visible above ground. The front part and the apse are not currently visible.
descriptions.NUR12634:
It is located in the territory of the comune of Decimoputzu (CA).

I° Giants' tomb with stele, dated to the Middle Bronze Age I (XVI–XV)

II° Neolithic tomb

III° Punic burial
descriptions.NUR12235: Two opposing dolmenic tombs. One has been excavated and consists of two chambers, with the entrance facing south. The other is unexplored; its covering slabs are visible, and the entrance faces north.
descriptions.NUR12885: A Chalcolithic necropolis discovered by chance during public works for the new Cagliari aqueduct. Three oven-type tombs were identified and investigated: of the first, found on the lowest part of the ridge on which the site extends, only the cell cut into the sandstone bedrock survived; 5 m to the west of the previous burial a second tomb preserved the vertical shaft and the oven-type cell with an elliptical plan intact.
descriptions.NUR15000: irregular and buried, whose structure cannot be defined
descriptions.NUR14986: It is located near the Nuragic spring on Musuleu. It appears to be a Nuragic-period structure.
descriptions.NUR19236: In this sacred well, of which nothing more is known and which was probably destroyed, several bronze figurines of considerable importance were found, including the standard above the votive sword and the warrior with shield and four daggers.
descriptions.NUR19984: A rocky ridge overlooking the Villasimius promontory, Capo Boi, the Campus valley, and Is Cuccureddus, where the Nuragic village and later the Temple of Astarte stood. Dry-stone walls, typically Nuragic, were built across the crevices. Around them it is easy to find terracotta kiln waste and a few Nuragic potsherds.
descriptions.NUR8639: Archaeological site of Mont'e Prama, where statues, baetyls, and the linear necropolis of pozzetto tombs have been found.
descriptions.NUR19629: Area where nuragic huts are found
descriptions.NUR19415: Situated in the Bèrchida valley, it shows use and occupation from the Nuragic period, with a substantial surface scatter of pottery fragments of Middle-Late Imperial date. It was inhabited until the 1950s. Among the dwelling remains, the ruins of a small religious building are of particular interest; it is already attested in 14th-century documentation.
descriptions.NUR19545: The village, lying east of the two nuraghi, occupies a broad flat area and consists of several structures. An apsidal hut is visible, rectangular in plan with a forecourt vestibule, in good condition, together with a probable circular hut and two enclosures. The area covered by the village is currently being excavated, bringing further structures to light. The structures were certainly reused up to recent times.
descriptions.NUR19645: In this locality the remains of an extensive settlement with an associated necropolis are clearly visible. From the material found in this citadel it emerges that it was inhabited from the earliest times of the Bonnanaro, Ozieri, Monte Claro and Bell Beaker cultures, and then by the Nuragic, Phoenician-Punic and Roman peoples. It seems the village was inhabited until 500 AD and was abandoned following a fire that caused its destruction.
descriptions.NUR19734: De Chirigu Village, the one to the north-west of the nuraghe of the same name, even though immersed in dense vegetation, shows several clearly distinguishable wall stretches belonging to probable huts, mostly rectangular in shape. At the far end, to the north-north-west, there is a circular structure (diameter about 10 m) that probably served as a meeting hut, against whose south side a rectangular structure is abutted. Numerous pottery fragments from various periods are present.
descriptions.NUR19810:
Sa Pedra de Nunnale – Orune. A village built around the picturesque and colossal tower of bizarre shape, at the base of which stands the eponymous Nuraghe. The nuraghe, though imposing, appears incredibly tiny compared with the immense rock that looms over it.

This single-tower nuraghe is built of megalithic blocks only roughly dressed, of even larger dimensions at the base
descriptions.NUR14796: Ugas mentions this site as a probable village and workshop of the pre-Nuragic period. Along the regular furrows of ploughing, still today, fragments of pottery, obsidian, and remains of lithic hammers are found.
descriptions.NUR2407: Single-tower nuraghe and remains of huts and giants' tomb.
descriptions.NUR14881: Nuraghe and village, of which only faint traces remain
descriptions.NUR16203: Scattered across the area are various structures of the probable village, in some cases consisting of only a few courses of pseudo-walls, with boulders still in their original position and collapse inside the perimeter. Unfortunately, because of the collapse and the dense, luxuriant vegetation of wild olive, mastic, phillyrea, etc., it is not possible to determine their type or size. Numerous potsherds lie on the surface of the area.
descriptions.NUR19727:
Situated at the foot of a hill along the course of the Rio Caddare, in an area covered by dense vegetation, the remains of wall structures belonging to the village can be seen emerging from a section of the hill eroded by the elements; these are not, however, the only evidence relating to this settlement.

Venturing into the vegetation it is in fact possible to identify the presence on the ground of numerous circular structures.
descriptions.NUR17569: Village attached to the nuraghe Lu Padru
descriptions.NUR12864:
On the northern outskirts of Selargius, in the locality of Su Coddu, lies an important Neolithic settlement where the remains of over 150 huts and artefacts belonging to the village have been found; it appears to have extended over 10 hectares.

These are traces of a Neolithic settlement (3000 BC), consisting of about thirty archaeological deposits belonging to the Ozieri/Monte Claro Culture.
descriptions.NUR3750: The Nuragic complex of Tamùli is an important archaeological site dating to the Middle Bronze Age (1500–1200 BC). The site was already well known in the first half of the nineteenth century, thanks largely to the description given by the scholar General Alberto Della Marmora in his Voyage en Sardaigne, published in 1840. In the accompanying atlas he illustrated the nuraghe, two of the three giants' tombs present, the baetyls and several ashlars on the spot with numerous drawings.
descriptions.NUR5492: The Nuragic settlement comprises about a hundred circular huts distributed without any apparent order at regular intervals from one another. It is built with regular courses of limestone blocks; the rare trachyte blocks probably come from the nearby Monte Imberi. The huts, circular (diameter 6–7 m), are for the most part currently covered by collapse debris and overgrown with dense Mediterranean maquis.
descriptions.NUR14840: It is a hilltop settlement, near a natural spring, inhabited by Nuragic peoples of the Late Bronze Age (1300–1200 BC), practically destroyed by agricultural work. Surface finds have yielded evidence of metallurgical activity documented by a hoard containing fragments of copper cakes and oxhide ingots from the island of Cyprus in the eastern Mediterranean.
descriptions.NUR11356:
On the site and in the surrounding area there are several alignments formed by large basalt blocks and at least two large clearance cairns resulting from the destruction of structures during agricultural work carried out in the past in the area.

Obsidian flakes and knapping debris outcrop near a path and in the exposed section relating to the left-hand side of the same, to the north of the Temannu nuraghe.
descriptions.NUR12865: The settlement is characterised by the presence of a village, documented by pockets of deposits and hut foundations, attributable to the Nuragic age, more specifically to the Middle Bronze, Recent Bronze, Final Bronze and Early Iron Age phases. The Recent Bronze Age phases are attested, for the most part, by the numerous finds of grey-slate pottery made in the 1980s at the same time as the site was first reported.
descriptions.NUR14819: The protohistoric settlement of Via Monastir–Via S. Giovanni in San Sperate extends over an area in the present north-eastern sector of the modern Campidano town. It was identified at several points within the same UGAS; it developed along the interfluvial strip between the north bank of the Riu Flumineddu and the south bank of the Riu Mannu, at elevations not exceeding 46 m above sea level.
descriptions.NUR9529: Likely corridor nuraghe and remains of a Nuragic settlement
descriptions.NUR1889: Village of which only little or nothing remains due to construction, down to the immediately surrounding areas.
descriptions.NUR19412: The village lies on the slope of Capo Su Moru, north-west of Torre Canai. The area is strewn with trachyte blocks of various sizes and, in stretches where the Mediterranean scrub is less dense, quadrangular and circular wall traces can be glimpsed, signalling the probable presence of a village, if not a temple.
descriptions.NUR18115: In a SSE direction from the Chentugheddas nuraghe, at a distance of more than 200 m from it, portions of the foundations of several circular-plan huts survive, forming a settlement whose occupied area cannot be estimated. On the surface, near the huts, a good quantity of Nuragic pottery is visible.
descriptions.NUR15643:
The existence of the village, belonging to the nearby nuraghe of the same name, is attested by the presence of a few circular huts and other alignments of stones emerging from the ground.

The settlement lies in the municipal territory of Macomer (NU).
descriptions.NUR3494: Approximate area of the Nuragic village Codula Manna
descriptions.NUR19538: A village composed of numerous huts, almost all overgrown with dense vegetation that nevertheless allows their partial structure to be seen. In several cases parts of the huts' perimeter walls are visible. On the plateau at the top of the hill there are a few buildings, one of which in particular preserves a rectangular room with a circular enclosure; given its state of preservation it has been used in recent times as an animal shelter. Pottery sherds are present.
descriptions.NUR19732: The Nuragic village next to the nuraghe cannot be defined in its structure because of the massive collapse. To the north-west, about 350 m from the nuraghe, there is a village which, although immersed in vegetation and fronted by a considerable collapse, presents: several huts whose wall structure is clearly visible; many stretches of cyclopean walls defining enclosures of various sizes. Numerous pottery fragments belonging to various periods are present.
descriptions.NUR16153: South-south-east of the nuraghe of the same name lies the village, where enclosures and walls can be seen. In some cases the surviving wall structure is rectangular; in others, barely outlined, it appears circular. It should be noted that almost all the structures are overgrown with a thicket of wild olives.
descriptions.NUR11926:
It is a large village, presumably of the Monte Claro Culture (Cagliari), which spread in Sardinia around the second half of the third millennium BC. In the centre of the polygon, because of land reclamation, little of the village walling remains, while on the two far sides traces of huts with rectangular and circular plans still emerge.

The plan in photo no. 6 was provided by the archaeologist who directed the excavations.
descriptions.NUR14850: Nuragic village of the recent and final Bronze Age I period
descriptions.NUR11309: Wall alignments and structural remains, among which a hut with a sub-rectangular plan is recognisable, surviving to a maximum height of about 1 m, built of small basalt blocks laid dry, with a small lintelled window. Modern and contemporary enclosures stand in the area of the concentration. The area of what was presumably a settlement extends around the nuraghe Marzacche.
descriptions.NUR16326: According to legend, it was one of the seven villages destroyed because of the beautiful Maria Cadelana.
descriptions.NUR10808: Nuragic village where 32 settlement structures dug deep into the ground, a nuraghe, a silver quarry and pre-Nuragic finds have been found. The site was covered with concrete in the 1980s to create a large irrigation tank that never went into operation.
descriptions.NUR17766: It is a large village, showing a spread of ruins, with nuraghe walls covering an area of about eight thousand square metres.
descriptions.NUR17759: Little of the village survives; only the ruins of huts emerge, and I believe this was the ordinary settlement, while a short distance away stands the namesake Sanctuary and Temple, with the adjacent Village of Nuragic huts partly still standing; I think these were the (Cumbissias), inhabited only on the occasion of periodic feast days or pagan rites.
descriptions.NUR20127:
The village lies a few metres south of the nuraghe of the same name, on top of Su Monte 'e Subra. Once you reach the summit you are faced with a vast expanse of stones and ashlars covering at least two hectares.

As you approach the various mounds, circular structures, rectangular structures, complex buildings, long walls and ramparts begin to emerge. The site has never been excavated.
descriptions.NUR8160: The village includes three sacred wells and a series of circular huts. The best-preserved well lies in the northern sector of the area. Built of medium-sized blocks of local schist, it abuts a small natural rock face to the south-west. Access to the chamber is off-centre relative to the axis of the tholos. The tholos has collapsed on its northern side. The area in front of the entrance chamber is bounded by a series of curvilinear walls at different levels.
descriptions.NUR14875: Today at least 12 sites with evidence of the Final Bronze Age II – Early Iron Age (S'Urbale and Genna Maria facies) are counted in the territory of Serrenti... All except one are settlements that were already active from the Recent Bronze Age. Only at Is Arruinalis, Monti Angurdu and Monti Crastu do we also find evidence of the Orientalising and Archaic phases (7th–6th centuries BC).
descriptions.NUR17873: Currently, nuragic huts remain with very little, only heaps of stone in circular and square shapes, probably the result of clearing works.
descriptions.NUR1593: The Nuragic village of Neulè is located in the area of the same name, a few kilometres from the settlement of Dorgali. The site includes numerous intact huts, a sacred well, and a nuraghe.
descriptions.NUR10697: Nuragic settlement of Pidighi. On the rocky ridge around the Pidighi nuraghe, for a radius of at least 50 metres, the remains of the Nuragic village are clearly visible among the basalt outcrops and the scrub.
descriptions.NUR14978: The village of Sa Muralla, whose name comes from the late medieval walls built around the village and the Castle in 1365, may be linked to the ancient toponym "Nuragonnos" on the northern outskirts of Sanluri; the latter probably referred to the hills on which the present town stands, perhaps already inhabited during the pre-Nuragic Monte Claro phase, as indicated by the Cukkuru Poddinis hypogeum.
descriptions.NUR14833: It is a large area of archaeological interest and lies near the ruins of a country church that are visible in the territory of Sanluri, just beyond the border with our village. It saw a succession of prehistoric settlements, datable from the Middle Bronze Age (16th–14th century BC) to the Iron Age (9th–8th century BC).
descriptions.NUR20356: A village without a nuraghe. From the same area comes a Copper Age dagger with a leaf-shaped blade, and a pink trachyte basin with a rim diameter of 70 cm. The presence of a bronze hoard at Sant'Elia is noted; it has been lost and was reported by Giuseppe Atzori.
descriptions.NUR20108: It lies in the locality of the same name, about 1.5 km as the crow flies from the SP165. Easily reached by farm tracks, the village covers about two hectares. Among the ruins are several structures occupying the whole area within the visible boundaries of the complex. Some appear to be huts, others are larger and more like enclosures.
descriptions.NUR2343: The Seruci Nuragic complex consists of a multi-lobed nuraghe with five towers and a central courtyard, and a village of about a hundred huts covering five hectares in a strategic position overlooking the Gulf of Leone. The village is organised into small quarters with streets and central squares. Of particular interest is a hut of remarkable size, probably used for meetings of the heads of families.
descriptions.NUR542: Complex nuraghe consisting of three towers standing in a line, perched on the rocky peak of Monte Sirimagus, one of which has a well cut into the rock. All around is a village with dozens of huts surrounded by as many as three enclosing walls. The site has been extensively disturbed by tomb robbers. At the foot of the mountain a perennial pond was used in the Nuragic period.
descriptions.NUR20036: STESSEI, indeed almost against the nuraghe on the east side, the remains of a Nuragic village are clearly visible, covering an area of at least ten thousand square metres and consisting of numerous huts partly hidden among piles of stones. Among the huts there are at least three wells (or cisterns).
descriptions.NUR11965: It is a large Nuragic village, currently only a small amount remains; only the presence of mounds and scattered stones around the homonymous nuraghe can be observed.
descriptions.NUR18380:
Comprises one hundred reoccupied nuragic huts in Roman period.

Near the village there is also a nuragic well and it appears that there are some menhirs.
descriptions.NUR11930: Beautiful village surrounded by a megalithic wall.
descriptions.NUR14861: Nuragic village inhabited in Final Bronze II and Iron I, without any nuraghe.
descriptions.NUR19631: The Nuragic village of Grutti acqua lies on the plateau in front of the complex nuraghe and consists of numerous circular and rectangular huts. Unfortunately only ruins of the huts survive, and moreover almost all of them are completely covered by dense vegetation that nevertheless allows the structure to be identified, albeit partially.
descriptions.NUR13475: Nuraghe belonging to the type dated to the 14th century BC; a few dozen metres away lies the funerary area; the village, divided into two sectors: one residential and the other artisanal. Dozens of circular huts blend in among the natural rocks.
descriptions.NUR8745: Possible uninvestigated Nuragic village. The TdG area contained 80 skeletons.
descriptions.NUR19721: While still a student, Giovanni Lilliu reported the presence of twenty circular and elliptical huts, some of which were later excavated, yielding ceramic materials of various kinds such as large jars, bowls, copper beads, and a bronze figurine depicting two oxen found during agricultural work. Despite the destruction, the emerging remains of some walls, large fragments of furnishings, and large fragments of basalt querns are still on the ground.
descriptions.NUR12736:
Nuragic village near Monte Maiori, in the municipality of Guspini.

A fascinating place because it is immersed in nature. It was certainly re-used by local shepherds but it keeps its history alive.

It is not the only one in this municipality.
descriptions.NUR19855: The probable Nuragic village occupies an area to the south-east of Monte Oliena. It consists of several structures, most likely reused over the centuries. In particular, a heavily damaged structure composed of several rectangular rooms can be seen. A series of circular and rectangular huts can also be identified, of which traces remain, in some cases two or three courses of perimeter walls.
descriptions.NUR19747: At the foot of the nuraghe of the same name – in the east-south-east sector – wall remains probably belonging to the village are visible, though partly hidden by the scrub. One can clearly make out: the entrance to an enclosure; the remains of a rectangular hut; cyclopean walls adjoining the hut structures and the nuraghe itself. The structures were almost certainly reused in relatively recent times.
descriptions.NUR5667: The site contains, in the inner face of the wall, a room of probable domestic use and the so-called dentilled stele of a giants' tomb. The stele, finely worked, was reused in Roman times and confirms the certain presence of a Nuragic funerary structure of the coursed type in isodomic masonry, whose original position has not yet been identified.
descriptions.NUR21152: A large area belonging to a probable Nuragic village. In the surrounding areas potsherds and other surface finds are easily found. The village extends a good way south from the indicated point and towards the stream to the west.
descriptions.NUR19670: The probable Nuragic village consists of several huts of which only shapeless remains survive. In some cases walls made of several courses (3–5) of boulders of various sizes remain. Most of the buildings are overgrown by vegetation whose growth has damaged their structure; where the structures lie in open ground the remains are indecipherable to the eye.
descriptions.NUR14893: Nuraxi – Pauli Onigus shows few and uncertain traces of a settlement in its immediate vicinity, while remains of a village can be seen at Pauli Onigus, a locality about 200 m to the south but separated by the course of the Riu Cardaxu. The extent of the villages, based on the materials visible on the surface, almost always varies between 7,000 and 10,000 sq m, apart from the village of Is Arruinalis, with remains mostly of the BFII-FI phase, which covers an area of about 4 hectares.
descriptions.NUR12019: Through a wild gully carved by a stream in the porphyritic granite, access is gained to the Nuragic village of Praidas. The remains are in severe disrepair and have significantly collapsed.
descriptions.NUR17280: The village was enclosed by a megalithic wall.
descriptions.NUR16965: The village lies at the foot of Monte Perdas de Fogu, in the locality Sa Costa de su Lurdagu. The structures survive as disordered wall remains; in some cases two rows of boulders are arranged in a pseudo-circular form. All the structures contain fallen boulders and rubble inside, making it difficult to determine their original perimeter and shape. Numerous potsherds of various kinds are visible on the surface throughout the area.
descriptions.NUR12521: Nuragic settlement area. A nuragic station has been identified with clear signs of human presence (about 1300 BC).
descriptions.NUR14981: Around the parish church the remains of an important settlement have come to light, including three wells and Hut 5, interpreted as a council hall. The discovery of terracotta casting moulds in the area outside "Hut 4" proves that metal artefacts were produced on the spot. By the threshold of "Hut 1", also of the Final Bronze Age, a clay bowl containing ox-hide ingots was found, deposited in the Iron Age.
descriptions.NUR15219: Nuragic village lying south-south-east of the eponymous nuraghe. In the area concerned one can see courses of cyclopean walls and the remains of at least one probable hut. The lush vegetation growing there, mostly mastic shrubs, makes it impossible to trace the outline of other probable wall structures. Ceramic fragments are visible on the ground near these structures.
descriptions.NUR20339:
In some publications it is actually distinguished from the village and necropolis of Porcili Mannu, but the area is that of Sa Sucraxia and the local inhabitants refer to it by that name.

Almost hidden among the large trees, clearly visible remains of a large stone village can be seen, with several buildings, some dwellings, remains of tombs and other structures that cannot be more closely identified.
descriptions.NUR14897: Twenty-two Nuragic villages, large and small, are known in the municipal area, and not all were occupied at the same time. They are often found near a nuraghe, as at the Bruncu Pubusa site; in other cases (Giuanni Acca, Sattu Divisu, Bruncu Abis and Sa Serra) they lack one.
descriptions.NUR5542: The complex, consisting of the nuraghe and its village, is therefore incorporated within the present-day settlement, surrounded by a terraced park rich in fruit trees, aromatic herbs and Mediterranean scrub. It was built during the Middle Bronze Age (about 1700–1350 BC) on a small rise overlooking the Rio Carrabusu valley.
descriptions.NUR10715: Attached to granitic rocks are visible the remains of a Nuragic village near an abandoned old courtyard.
descriptions.NUR19764: The probable Nuragic village consists of several structures that were almost certainly reused up to the last century. The huts, whose remains can be glimpsed, were probably originally circular and rectangular in shape. Parts of the walls survive, built of semi-worked stones of varying sizes. The very dense vegetation, which in places has grown inside the structures, has contributed to their collapse. About 200 m to the east lies the Noccus pond.
descriptions.NUR19866: The probable Nuragic village occupies a large area on the eastern slope of the channel called S'ega Langonis. Despite the dense vegetation, more than 30 circular and rectangular huts can be counted. All have collapsed or imploded, partly because of illicit digging; even so, several courses of the perimeter walls survive on some of them. All the structures were built of small- and medium-sized polyhedral boulders, laid dry in more or less regular courses.
descriptions.NUR19762: The probable Nuragic village consists of several huts of which linear wall remains survive, formed by several courses (in some cases up to five) of stones of various sizes. They were probably rectangular structures. Unfortunately, dense and tangled vegetation conceals most of the structures. To the north, about 100 metres away, lies the Noccus pond, a water reserve for the villages in the area.
descriptions.NUR19535: The area contains the remains of numerous huts belonging to a Nuragic settlement; some of them were probably reused in later, though still remote, times. Most of the huts are circular and preserve only a few traces of the original structure: some have two or three discontinuous courses, others just a single course, of polyhedral boulders of various sizes. In the north-east sector there is an enclosure containing one rectangular hut divided into two rooms.
descriptions.NUR8716:
The complex, one of the most important and best preserved in Nuragic Sardinia, comprises a village-sanctuary with about a hundred huts, two small temples with adjoining enclosures, and two megalithic burials.

The village consists of isolated huts and clusters of huts arranged around central spaces. Six groupings can be counted, some equipped with well-cisterns and small wells connected to water channels. The huts, circular, are built of drystone masonry with irregular courses.
descriptions.NUR19253: It lies in the territory of Pozzomaggiore (SS), near the nuraghe (proto-nuraghe) Sinadorzu or Scale e Ozzastru; there are several huts and enclosure walls, and nearby one can see probable remains of giants' tombs and perhaps a Nuragic sacred well, obviously all in deplorable condition.
descriptions.NUR12567: Submerged Nuragic village noted by Pierluigi Montalbano in public conferences
descriptions.NUR20064: Hundreds upon hundreds of ruins, huts and towers linked by little lanes, catapult us back thousands of years, showing how imposing and important this site was in the Nuragic period. Two things stand out in particular. The first is a kind of amphitheatre, a majestic horseshoe-shaped building; the other is the spring.
descriptions.NUR19656: A village composed of several circular huts of which only a few courses and the collapsed structure in the centre remain, plus two of complex structure. Of these two, the first, rectangular, consists of five rooms: four roughly circular ones at the four sides and one rectangular one in the centre, perhaps a courtyard; the second, oval, has four rooms, three of them round and the fourth formed by the wall joining the three rooms, perhaps a courtyard. Enclosures with cyclopean walls are present.
descriptions.NUR16077: Village – scattered across the area are several stretches of walling that may belong to the village huts; unfortunately the dense vegetation does not allow a broad view of the area and makes it difficult to identify the structures.
descriptions.NUR19654: The probable Nuragic village occupies an area that extends from the edges of the plateau down the NE slope of the mountain. There are remains of several circular huts of which one or two courses and the collapsed structure in the centre survive. The best preserved is an oval hut, very probably reused in more recent times. Enclosures with cyclopean walls are present.
descriptions.NUR11737: Excavations carried out in 1997 brought to light several huts of various plans bounded by orthostatic slabs and with their associated hearths. The archaeological layers yielded abundant ceramic remains, some metal objects and bone artefacts, now kept in the Teti Archaeological Museum. The site is dated from the Middle Bronze Age III to the early Iron Age.
descriptions.NUR19718: On a small rise on the eastern side of the Monte Ozzatru stream, which joins the Caddare stream a few dozen metres away, numerous heaps of stones can be seen, presumably the result of field clearance, and in the immediate vicinity fragments of Nuragic pottery and a fragmentary granite quern emerge from the ground.
descriptions.NUR11931: Here there was a Nuragic village, of which only faint traces remain.
descriptions.NUR12030: Nuragic village composed of about 30 huts, and at a short distance there was a sacred well.
descriptions.NUR11458:
The village of "Cuccuru Ambudu" extended over a broad hilly area (61 m a.s.l.) on the north-eastern outskirts of Serramanna, between the roads leading west to Serrenti and east to Villagreca.

The characteristics of the village, reconstructed through careful analysis of the finds, suggest it was already occupied in the pre-Nuragic period, in a phase datable between the Late Neolithic (Ozieri Culture) and the Chalcolithic (Monte Claro Culture).
descriptions.NUR15127: Contiguous with the area where the corridor nuraghe of the same name stands, it consists of dozens of quadrangular huts, sometimes divided into several rooms and apsidal, bounded by blocks set on edge. Sometimes affected by illegal excavations, the fragile pre-Nuragic dwellings are located both inside the wooded area owned by the municipality and, in greater numbers, outside it, in a large area used as pasture.
descriptions.NUR11033: At the end of the Geometric phase the number of occupied sites continues to fall: evidence for the 7th and 6th centuries BC is found only at Monti Crastu, Is Arruinalis and Monti Angurdu, where decorated sherds of the Archaic phase have been observed. In this later phase it is likely that the centre of Is Arruinalis grew to a “proto-urban” level, as is known to have happened at other settlements in the Campidano and Marmilla (Tuppedili, San Sperate).
descriptions.NUR1868: The area contains the remains of more than ten huts belonging to a Nuragic settlement. The village area has been completely altered, I would say devastated, during the Second World War, when the structures belonging to most of the huts were dismantled or adapted into military positions.
descriptions.NUR1800: The nuraghe stands on the Gullei. It is a single enormous lava flow several kilometres long. The village is not easy to reach because it is wrapped in dense wild scrub. The nuraghe is a three-lobed one whose walls are visible. For at least one or two hectares around, the village spreads out, with a furnace, a well and more besides. From the top of the towers the whole territory and the coast are visible as far as the Mariolu cliffs to the south and Cala Ginepro to the north.
descriptions.NUR18947: Nuragic huts possibly associated with both nuraghes in the vicinity
descriptions.NUR8111: Nestled in the Lanaitto valley, the village of Sa Sedda e Sos Carros (literally “the crossing point of the carts”) dates from a period between the Recent Bronze Age and the Early Iron Age (12th–9th centuries BC). It is particularly important for the presence of traces of metal smelting and working in the Nuragic period. It consists of numerous huts, with circular and oval plans, among which one is of particular interest for its ritual religious function.
descriptions.NUR19723: On a mountain terrace at the foot of the Ischiriddé pinnacle stood the village of Sas Funtanas, a very short distance from the Duas Vuccas cave. Lilliu reports the discovery of fragments of millstones and hand-mills and of a two-handled olla containing a copper chisel, and notes the presence of the small village, which is no longer visible today because of the dense vegetation.
descriptions.NUR18807: In the literature, just as on the ground, Su Padrigheddu is closely linked to the S'Uraki nuraghe complex, first mentioned as such by A. Taramelli in 1935. The finds were immediately attributed to a village, settled in the Nuragic period and occupied continuously down to the Republican Roman period.
descriptions.NUR20007: From the upper level of the nuraghe in the north-east, a view of the village is visible, with huts still discernible amid thick vegetation and among the various collapses.
descriptions.NUR12860: Nuragic settlement with particular attention to the lithic industry. Among other finds, polished stone axes, hammers and mace-heads have been found here. One of the most unusual finds is a depiction of a dagger on pottery.
descriptions.NUR1818: Location of the remains of the Tattari Pizzinnu nuraghe, of which only the foundations remain, a Roman villa built with stones from the nuraghe, and the remaining Roman-period settlement.
